title: Zero Slope: Why a Horizontal Line Has Slope 0

scenes.title: Why is a horizontal line's slope zero?
body: The line moves sideways, but it never moves up or down.
scenes.narration: Suppose a line passes through negative three, four and five, four. What is its slope? Here is the idea: slope measures vertical change compared with horizontal change. This line moves eight units to the right, but its height never changes. That is exactly what zero slope means.

scenes.title: The confusion: zero is not undefined
body: Slope = change in y divided by change in x.
Zero on top gives slope 0; zero on the bottom would be undefined.
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. A zero numerator and a zero denominator are completely different. Here, change in y is four minus four, which is zero. Change in x is five minus negative three, which is eight. So the slope is zero divided by eight, and that equals zero. Undefined slope happens when the denominator is zero, not the numerator.

scenes.title: What slope 0 actually means
body: As x changes, y stays constant.
No rise and no fall means a horizontal line.
scenes.narration: Notice the meaning, not just the calculation. If x changes but y stays constant, there is no rise and no fall. The rate of change is zero. So every horizontal line has slope zero. For this example, the line is y equals four: whatever x you choose, y remains four.

scenes.title: Quick check with another pair
scenes.narration: Let us verify with two different points on the same line: zero, four and two, four. The change in y is still zero, while the change in x is two. Zero divided by two is zero again. The result does not depend on which two distinct points you choose on a horizontal line.

scenes.title: Horizontal line → slope 0
body: y = 4 has the same output everywhere.
Remember: 0 over a nonzero number is 0.
scenes.narration: So the big idea is simple: slope asks how much y changes when x changes. On a horizontal line, y does not change at all, so the slope is zero. And remember the common mistake: zero on top gives zero slope; zero on the bottom gives undefined slope. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT. Find the complete lesson below.
